name: Executive Order of July 18, 1876 restoring the 1874 Jicarilla reserve to the public domain (Royce area 563)
promises: Not a treaty: a presidential order. It restored to the public domain the tract set apart for the Jicarilla by executive order of March 25, 1874 (Royce p. 886).

The Indian Claims Commission found the 1874 reservation lay at the headwaters of the San Juan River in Colorado near the Utes, that the Jicarilla refused to go onto it, and that it was abolished by this order (finding 54, 1963).
today: The Commission found in 1963 that the Jicarilla were gradually deprived of their aboriginal lands without compensation, moved from one reservation to another until the executive order of February 1, 1887 gave them their present reservation; the land claim ended in a stipulated final award of $9,150,000.00 on April 21, 1971 (Docket 22-A). Those findings concern aboriginal title, not this order.

openQuestions: An executive order taking back executive-order land is not a breach by itself (Jordan, 2026-11-08); the Commission mentions this order but makes no finding that it took Jicarilla land, and the 1874 reserve lay in Colorado, which may be outside the Jicarilla award area (not plotted).
The 1971 award was entered on a stipulation (a settlement), so it is recorded here as context only.
The Jicarilla Apache Nation's own account was not found (its website did not respond).
